extracted.intended_audience: graduate students, scholars, and historians/philosophers of science; scientists interested in conceptual foundations of scientific change
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and assess the features that indicate a transition from normal to extraordinary science and the conditions under which one scientific paradigm is replaced by an incompatible successor. Emphasizes anomalies, community dynamics, conceptual change, and the role of persuasive argumentation versus purely logical or experimental adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought experiments expose paradigm failure
rubrics_metrics.description: The analytical thought experimentation ... is perfectly calculated to expose the old paradigm to existing knowledge in ways that isolate the root of crisis with a clarity unattainable in the laboratory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use thought experiments to reveal tensions between paradigm expectations and known facts; they can identify the core of a crisis more clearly than routine experiments. (Kuhn cites Galileo, Einstein, Bohr.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraordinary procedures concentrate attention on anomalies
rubrics_metrics.description: By concentrating scientific attention upon a narrow area of trouble and by preparing the scientific mind to recognize experimental anomalies for what they are, crisis often proliferates new discoveries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing periods of extraordinary research, look for focused efforts on problematic areas and increased sensitivity to anomalies; such concentration often produces multiple discoveries (examples: Lavoisier from Priestley, optical discoveries before the wave theory of light).

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of crisis fosters discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: The awareness of crisis distinguishes Lavoisier’s work on oxygen from Priestley’s; ... new optical discoveries accumulated rapidly just before and during the emergence of the wave theory of light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that explicit acknowledgment of anomaly/crisis within a community can catalyze discovery. In evaluating work, note whether researchers treat anomalies as problems requiring new conceptual schemes rather than as isolated errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: New paradigm may be foreshadowed by anomaly structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes the shape of the new paradigm is foreshadowed in the structure that extraordinary research has given to the anomaly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the anomalous data have been organized in ways that hint at a coherent alternative framework; such structuring can precede articulation of a full paradigm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Youth or newcomer status facilitates paradigm invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Almost always the men who achieve these fundamental inventions of a new paradigm have been either very young or very new to the field whose paradigm they change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When considering origins of innovative proposals, note the role of relative independence from prior commitments; newcomers or younger researchers may be less constrained by existing rules and more likely to propose radical alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symptoms of transition to extraordinary research
rubrics_metrics.description: The proliferation of competing articulations, the willingness to try anything, the expression of explicit discontent, the recourse to philosophy and to debate over fundamentals, all these are symptoms of a transition from normal to extraordinary research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this symptom set as indicators that a community is in crisis: look for multiple competing theories, methodological experimentation, explicit criticism of prevailing assumptions, and increased philosophical debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific revolutions are non-cumulative replacements
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific revolutions ... are those non-cumulative developmental episodes in which an older paradigm is replaced in whole or in part by an incompatible new one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess candidate revolutions by whether the change is incompatible and non-cumulative (i.e., the old paradigm must be rejected rather than simply extended). Examples: Copernican, Lavoisier, Newtonian→Einsteinian shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revolution inaugurated by sense of malfunction
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific revolutions are inaugurated by a growing sense ... that an existing paradigm has ceased to function adequately in the exploration of an aspect of nature to which that paradigm itself had previously led the way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate historical or contemporary claims of revolution by checking for a community-recognized sense that established methods/institutions/paradigms fail to address new problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigm choice cannot be decided solely by normal-science procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice between competing paradigms proves to be a choice between incompatible modes of community life. ... When paradigms enter ... into a debate about paradigm choice, their role is necessarily circular. Each group uses its own paradigm to argue in that paradigm’s defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging competing theories, account for social and rhetorical elements: normal-scientific evaluative procedures are themselves paradigm-dependent and thus cannot alone settle paradigm disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community assent as ultimate adjudicator
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no standard higher than the assent of the relevant community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating whether a paradigm has been accepted, prioritize whether the relevant scientific community assents to it (via practice, teaching, publication, persuasion), not only abstract logical or probabilistic proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anomalies, especially stubborn ones, give rise to new theories
rubrics_metrics.description: Only when these attempts at articulation fail do scientists encounter the ... recognized anomalies whose characteristic feature is their stubborn refusal to be assimilated to existing paradigms. This type alone gives rise to new theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat persistent, non-assimilable anomalies as the primary drivers for theory invention; assess whether purported anomalies truly resist assimilation rather than being due to experimental error or misinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Successful new theory must permit different predictions
rubrics_metrics.description: If new theories are called forth to resolve anomalies ... then the successful new theory must somewhere permit predictions that are different from those derived from its predecessor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate new theories by whether they make novel, testable predictions that diverge from the old paradigm and thereby allow discrimination between them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigms define methods, problems, and standards of solution
rubrics_metrics.description: Paradigms ... are the source of the methods, problem-field, and standards of solution accepted by any mature scientific community at any given time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing scientific work, consider how a paradigm prescribes what counts as a legitimate problem and acceptable solutions; a paradigm shift often redefines which questions are scientific and which are not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commitment to paradigm must extend beyond full precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: Without commitment to a paradigm there could be no normal science. Furthermore, that commitment must extend to areas and to degrees of precision for which there is no full precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that productive research requires a willingness to apply paradigmatic assumptions beyond strictly precedent cases; excessive skepticism about extrapolation can stifle problem selection and progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positivist restriction on theory range halts research
rubrics_metrics.description: If positivistic restrictions on the range of a theory’s legitimate applicability are taken literally, the mechanism that tells the scientific community what problems may lead to fundamental change must cease to function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of methodological prescriptions that limit theories strictly to observed domains; such restrictions prevent the speculative commitments necessary to generate anomalies and drive revolutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation of old theory from new is spurious without conceptual reinterpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Though the N1’s are a special case of the laws of relativistic mechanics, they are not Newton’s Laws. ... the physical referents of these Einsteinian concepts are by no means identical with those of the Newtonian concepts that bear the same name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claiming continuity between successive theories, examine whether key concepts retain the same referents; apparent derivations that change meanings are retrospective redefinitions and do not demonstrate genuine theoretical continuity for practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retrospective reinterpretation cannot guide research
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless we change the definitions of the variables in the N1’s, the statements we have derived are not Newtonian. If we do change them, we cannot properly be said to have derived Newton’s Laws ... the result ... would be a theory so restricted that it could only restate what was already known. ... it could not suffice for the guidance of research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between retrospective restatements of old theories in new terms and theories that actually guide future research; the former may have utility but cannot replace the role of paradigmatic guidance in choosing problems and methods.
